items.detail:
The prune this job added (`loop/run.mjs:1367`) closes the branch-deletion case for any run that reaches cleanup, but the same stale entry has a second effect the diff does not touch. `loop/lib/review.mjs:712` does `rmSync(reviewDir)` then `addWorktree(...)` at that exact path, and `loop/run.mjs:912` does the same for the job worktree — neither prunes first. Measured on a throwaway repo, git 2.40.0.windows.1: with a stale entry for a path whose directory was deleted, `git worktree add --detach <same path>` exits 128 with `fatal: '<path>' is a missing but already registered worktree; use 'add -f' to override, or 'prune' or 'remove' to clear`. `addWorktree` throws on a non-ok result (`loop/lib/git.mjs:91`), so that aborts the run. It cannot arise from a run that completes — the new prune clears it — only from one killed at the wall-clock cap after a failed `worktree remove`. One `gitTry(repo, ['worktree','prune'])` before each `addWorktree`, or the same trailing prune added to `review.mjs:752`, would close it.

items.detail:
The gemini-3-8-flash docket attributes two things to https://9to5google.com/2026/09/02/gemini-3-8-flash-launch/ that I could not reproduce from that page with my own extractor: Wiz's "+7.5-9.7% recall" (the page as I retrieved it says only "higher recall on their internal penetration testing benchmark for a 2.3-5.2x lower cost", with no percentage range), and the sentence "At times, the model might use more tokens to maximize performance, especially at higher effort levels" (I retrieved the adjacent "works harder" framing as "exhibit[s] greater diligence — executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively"). This is NOT a finding that either is wrong — WebFetch's extractor denies text that is present as readily as it invents text, so absence through it proves nothing, and every other figure in this docket reproduced exactly. It is a flag that these two are the only unconfirmed items in the set: the entry job that picks this candidate up should quote whichever sentence the page actually carries, and drop the percentage range if it is not there rather than carry it forward on the docket's authority.

items.detail:
2 findings carried by reviewers against `data/proposals/gpt-6-astra-release-system-card.md`, batched into one job because they concern the same file. Each is stated below in the reviewing reviewer's own words. Fix every one, or say in `RESULT.md` which you did not and why — a finding you leave standing must keep its file.

### Quote the Astra post's closing sentence in full, or mark the truncation

Carried in `data/carried/j-20260904-02-carry-1.md`.

The candidate's summary and why-now both say the site's own post "ends with the sentence 'Until the system card lands, the capability numbers are OpenAI's word.'" The sentence in content/blog/openai-astra-critical-designation.md:57 is longer — "Until the system card lands, the capability numbers are OpenAI's word, and the designation itself is the dated, checkable fact." The truncation drops the half that says the designation *was* checkable, which is the original post's actual position. Any post written from this docket should quote the whole sentence or ellipse the cut.

### Disambiguate FrontierMath Tier 4 97.6 vs 98 before the post prints either

Carried in `data/carried/j-20260904-02-carry-2.md`.

The candidate's evidence block quotes the release page's prose ("saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score") and its done-when line then lists "FrontierMath Tier 4 97.6/98" as if both were table rows. Vellum's benchmark write-up of the same release (fetched 2026-09-04, https://www.vellum.ai/blog/gpt-6-astra-benchmarks-explained) reports the table value as "FrontierMath Tier 4 (v2): Astra 97.6". The post should print 97.6 as the measured row and treat "98%" as the announcement's rounded prose, naming which is which — not print both as scores.

items.detail:
verify-daybreak-defense-network-product-wording.md says "a plain `user-agent`-only fetch returns HTTP 403 (Cloudflare challenge); the successful request sent `accept-language: en-US,en;q=0.9` and `cache-control: no-cache` alongside a full Chrome UA." That did not reproduce on 2026-09-04 from this machine: a fetch sending ONLY the same full Chrome `user-agent` returned HTTP 200 with 375,911 bytes, while a fetch sending no headers at all (Node's default UA) returned HTTP 403 with 9,861 bytes. So the header that clears the challenge is the UA alone; `accept-language` and `cache-control` were not load-bearing. The fix is to restate the note as "a fetch with no browser user-agent returns 403; sending a full Chrome UA returns 200", or to drop the causal claim and record only the headers that were sent. Nothing else in the file depends on this — the retrieval it describes reproduces exactly. Note that Cloudflare gating is IP- and time-dependent, so the author may well have observed the 403 they recorded; the note is unreliable as a general instrument claim rather than dishonest.

items.detail:
The evidence file's header says the raw transcript is a "node fetch+strip+count script, 2026-09-03; the huggingface.co/meta-models org page was fetched twice because its activity feed renders intermittently". Grepping "^=== https" over data/reviews/evidence/verify-meta-spark-weights-pending-status.raw.txt returns 11 fetch blocks and huggingface.co/meta-models appears exactly once (line 22). The underlying observation is real — that page's stripped length was 2556 in the transcript and 2548 when I fetched it myself minutes later — but as written the sentence describes a second fetch the transcript does not contain. Either capture both fetches, or say it plainly ("the page was fetched in both this run and the earlier one and rendered differently; only this run's is captured"). This is the same narrative-outruns-transcript shape the previous pass flagged, at much smaller scale, which is why it is carried rather than blocked on.
